The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and appropriate for its quiet, reflective tone. The "story time" of the main action—a single, brief crossing on a small cable ferry—closely matches the "real world time" it takes to read the piece (just a few minutes). 

Within the unhurried rhythm of this short crossing, the author skillfully uses **compression of time** during the silences between mother and son. Decades of family history, Jonas's childhood, the death of Henning four years ago, and the slow economic decline of the region are condensed into a few brief internal observations. This contrast—stretching out the quiet, physical details of a few minutes on the water while compressing years of grief and change into passing thoughts—perfectly mirrors the emotional weight hanging between the two characters.
